ch51.note: The old lord is Yamauchi Yōdō (1827–1872), the retired daimyō of Tosa and one of the “four wise lords” of the Restoration; Geikai Suikō, “the Drunken Lord of the Whale Sea,” was his own literary sobriquet, and here names a record kept in his circle. His parting line to the troops, ten nao samushi, jiai seyo (“the season is yet cold; take care of yourself”), became famous, and Itagaki has it recited to his men again below, where its weight is less the warning than the reminder that they march for their own lord.

The propaganda was real, and it worked. Itagaki Taisuke’s family, the Inui, held a tradition of descent from Itagaki Nobukata, a senior general of Takeda Shingen, the sixteenth-century warlord whose old capital was Kōfu; the family had taken the name Inui generations before after a disgrace. Marching to seize Kai, Itagaki restored the ancestral surname (by most accounts at Ōgaki, as here) and spread word that Shingen’s Imperial descendant was coming home, turning a province of Tokugawa sympathizers toward the new government almost overnight.

ch51.anchor: walking abroad in brocade by night
ch51.note: Kondō’s “Tang saying” is in fact older, from the Records of the Grand Historian: the warlord Xiang Yu, urged to hold the capital, answered that to be rich and honored and not return to one’s home country was “like walking by night in embroidered robes,” with no one to see. It is the perfect motto for a farmer’s son parading a daimyō’s palanquin through the villages he grew up in, and Kondō, who cannot read it in the original, has it exactly right.

A horo was a large cloak of cloth stretched over a light bamboo frame and worn on the back of a mounted warrior; filled by the wind it ballooned into a great bag that could turn a spent arrow and, more to the point, made its wearer conspicuous as a mark of rank. By this date it was purely ceremonial, an antique of the picture-scrolls, which is why Onobu knows it only from warrior-prints; that the shogun’s house should present one to Toshizō measures both the honor and its unreality.

The shoin-bangashira commanded one of the elite guard units of the shogun’s own household, an office of high standing among the direct bannermen. It is the post that carried Toshizō’s yoriai rank and the horo with it. His flat “Risen, is it” is the chapter’s quiet counterweight to Kondō’s delight in the same honors.

ch51.anchor: a manuscript called the Riin Shiwa
ch51.note: The Riin Shiwa (“Fireside Tales from the Hedge’s Shade”) is an actual memoir set down by Satō Jin, grandson of the Hino headman Satō Hikogorō and grandnephew of Toshizō, preserving the household’s recollections of the Shinsengumi men it had known from boyhood. Shiba quotes it directly for the Hino homecoming; the passages of Kondō crossing the garden and Toshizō with the horo are, unusually, eyewitness family record rather than the novelist’s invention.

For the campaign Kondō took a samurai alias, shedding the outlaw name the new government had put a price on; the sources give it variously as Ōkubo Tsuyoshi and, later at Nagareyama, Ōkubo Yamato, the form Shiba uses here. The disguise fooled no one for long: within weeks the government gazette was naming “Ōkubo Yamato (Kondō Isami)” as a chief of rebels.

ch51.anchor: a shogunal unit called the Nappa-tai
ch51.note: The Nappa-tai (“rape-leaf corps”) was a shogunal infantry battalion nicknamed for the drab green of its Western uniforms; it was quartered near Kanagawa on the Tōkaidō. Toshizō’s night ride to beg its help is the measure of how thin the Kōyō Chinbutai had worn: two hundred men at the start, already halved by desertion, hoping to borrow the best part of two thousand.

ch51.anchor: was one Inoue Taisuke, then thirteen
ch51.note: The detail is one of Shiba’s genealogical asides, tying the scene to living descendants. The boy was the nephew of Inoue Genzaburō, the Tama comrade and Sixth-Unit captain killed at the Fushimi magistrate’s office in the first days of the war; left behind here at the Satō house, he survived, and through a marriage into Okita Sōji’s family carried a thread of these men down to a household still at Tachikawa in the writer’s own day.
